_revised: 2026-09-05, same day: the transcription was faithful but the notes were stale. The two color-analysis files contradicted each other, the chino plan prescribed a Western-preppy slim cut that works against the stated goal, and nothing in the folder said what the target register actually is. This file now carries both layers and says which is which: fields marked as facts (size, brands) are still transcription; direction, palette, silhouette, hair and buyNext are a styling judgement made against photographs, and can be argued with.
_excluded: Appearance.md from the same folder is deliberately never transcribed here or anywhere in this repo: it names real people and must never enter a public project.
_undertone: RESOLVED 2026-09-05, by the gold-versus-silver test held at the face: silver clearly better, gold a definite no. That settles Dark Winter and closes the only question this file was carrying. Everything downstream of it was updated in the same pass — the warm neutrals (camel, cream, stone, khaki, chocolate, rust, olive, tan) are out of the palette, out of buyNext, out of the seasonal wardrobe and out of the chino roadmap; the cool accents are promoted from conditional to real. The one non-obvious casualty is the hair note, which had recommended softening the near-black to a warm brown. That recommendation was undertone-dependent and did not survive.
_gaps: The wardrobe direction is written against photographs, not a fitting. Anything about how a specific garment actually falls on him is unverified until something is tried on.

Outfit_Planner.md carried one entry, on Monday: white chunky sweater, 90s light denim, loafers, gold small hoop earrings, trench coat. It is kept here rather than transcribed because the earrings and the chunky-knit-plus-trench combination read as someone else's outfit — possibly Eunice's, possibly saved inspiration. The undertone test adds a small piece of evidence rather than proof: gold at the ear is the metal he just ruled out, and light 90s denim is a warm wash. Nothing is lost; it just should not stand as Philipp's Monday until he confirms it. The day-based planner it would have seeded was dropped entirely 2026-09-08 — outfit choice tracks the occasion (`looks`), not the weekday, and a Monday–Sunday table only repeated 'School day' five times and sat empty the other two.

Trouser model names shift every season. The chino plan holds the brands and the cut; the specific SKUs in the original note are already partly superseded and should be re-checked in store rather than trusted here.

direction.register: Modern preppy, elevated — mature, not collegiate
direction.thesis: The wardrobe he was already buying toward (Ralph Lauren, Suitsupply, Charles Tyrwhitt) stops being an exception and becomes the actual plan: tailored coats and knitwear over a collared shirt, chinos with a clean line, camel and khaki back in alongside the cool core. Preppy's usual signals — bright polos, popped collars, varsity branding — are exactly the collegiate register this avoids; the 2026 version of this look is described everywhere as sophisticated and mature rather than campus, and that is the half being kept.
direction.builtFrom: Three facts about him, not a look: colouring that is Dark Winter and high-contrast, a 25 cm waist-to-hip drop, and a face that reads a decade younger than the passport. Those decide the trouser cut and how far the styling may mature regardless of register; the palette itself is cool by test, with camel and khaki confirmed back in on his own report on 2026-09-06.
direction._history: Full record, repo-only — stripped from the built page, kept here because the project's own rule is to print disagreements rather than smooth them over, just not at the cost of the page's own readability. Rewritten twice. First written in Korean-actor vocabulary because that was asked for, then generalised — the palette, cut and hair never actually depended on the label, only the reference photos did. Then, on 2026-09-06, the register itself changed: from quiet, dark minimalism to modern preppy, and Gong Yoo, Hyun Bin and Park Seo-joon were genuinely accurate references for the old register specifically, not for this one. Gong Yoo got a second look before being dropped: as a person he is described as versatile — suits to streetwear, no preppy label — and the one look with real preppy DNA, the Goblin/Kim Shin cardigan-over-crewneck sweater set, belongs to a wealthy-immortal costume rather than to his own documented style. A fictional character's wardrobe is a thinner basis for a real style reference than an actor's own red-carpet choices, so it didn't survive the fuller look. Separately: two searches for an adult, non-idol Asian figure specifically labelled 'preppy' came back close to empty — the label attaches almost only to K-pop idols doing the collegiate version. Byeon Woo Seok was the one sourced exception; Beckham and Reynolds are who the same 2026 coverage names once the search isn't restricted to Asian figures.
direction.onTheOriginalFraming: Written first in Korean-actor vocabulary, then generalised — the palette, cut and hair depend on his own measurements and colouring, not the label. The register itself changed again on 2026-09-06, quiet minimalism to modern preppy; the old references matched the old register, not this one.
direction.ageRead: Reads early-to-mid 30s in photographs, not 43: full hairline, even skin tone, no deep static lines. The clothes are currently the oldest thing in the picture. That widens the range rather than narrowing it — the limiter is context (school, parent evenings, Germany), not the birth year, and over-mature styling would hand back years the face has not lost.

notThis.why: Sheer fabric, embellishment, stage pieces — the idol register.
Bright polos, popped collars, varsity, baseball caps — the campus version this register avoids.

direction.referencesNote: Byeon Woo Seok is sourced for the garment specifics; Beckham and Reynolds for silhouette and attitude only. Colour is already settled from his own skin and the metal test, not from a reference photo.

references.name: Byeon Woo Seok
references.why: Actor, not idol; Prada ambassador; documented in cable-knit-over-collared-shirt layering — the core preppy combination, executed adult rather than campus. Age and build read close to his own.

references.name: David Beckham
references.why: Named directly in 2026 coverage of the trend: 'blending traditional tailoring with casual, sporty elements'. Mature, not collegiate, and the sportswear-into-tailoring move matches a man who trains regularly.

references.name: Ryan Reynolds
references.why: Named in the same coverage: 'clean, polished ensembles with a touch of whimsy'. The whimsy is the one thing to leave behind — the register wanted here is quieter than his press-tour persona — but the clean, tailored-casual base is exactly it.

direction.readOfCurrentPhotos: Four photographs, four sets of functional clothing: sport tee, polo, sport tee, printed sweatshirt. Not a taste problem — a control problem. Nothing in the set is a chosen silhouette. What already works: the gum-sole Sambas, and navy, which appears in three of four and flatters in all three. What works against him: the printed sweatshirt (busy, boxy, adds volume exactly where the training is removing it) and visible athletic branding outside the gym.

hair.priority: The single biggest lever — roughly 60% of the effect is decided before any garment is chosen. Hair either rounds the face or lengthens it, and nothing worn below the collar can undo that.
hair.caption: Taper cut — textured length on top, tapered sides (not shaved), matte not glossy. Near-black stays.

imageStyle.prefix: Close-up portrait illustration in a graphic novel style — flat matte ink like a European or American adult graphic novel, not anime or webtoon. Bold clean black ink outlines of even weight, no cross-hatching, no soft cel-shading, no gradients, no glossy highlights on the hair or skin. Head and shoulders only, three-quarter angle. Plain white background, no scenery, no props. No text, no labels, no captions, no logos.
imageStyle.figure: Early-30s East Asian man, light-to-medium skin tone — not pale, not fair-skinned. Mature and quiet, calm expression, no smile. Near-black hair in a taper cut: textured length and natural volume on top, falling softly to one side with lift at the crown, sides tapered short and blended into the top — never shaved or clipped to skin — matte and textured throughout, never glossy or wet-look. Wearing a plain navy crew-neck knit, no visible branding.
imageStyle.suffix: Portrait orientation, roughly 3:4, head and shoulders filling most of the frame with a small margin.

hair.current: Already close to the target most days, per his own photos — taper sides, natural volume on top, a soft side part or a looser textured sweep depending on the day. The gap only shows right after a cut that goes too short and too flat: no taper, no crown lift, which rounds the face and takes height away until it grows back out.
hair.cut: Taper, not two-block/undercut. A two-block's sharp contrast between shaved sides and long top needs a trim every 2–3 weeks to hold its line — Asian hair regrows fast enough that skin-short sides read 'grown out' within two weeks. A taper has no hard line to lose, so it holds its shape 6–8 weeks between cuts and is closer to what he already wears day to day. Ask the barber for: taper on the sides, not a skin-short or clipper-guard-zero undercut, with 4–6 cm of textured length on top.
hair.shape: Side sweep with lift at the crown — the classic preppy part, and it does more for his face shape than the alternative. Not a middle part: that reads closer to K-drama/idol styling than to this register, and without a real perm it tends to sit flat over a normal hairline rather than lengthening it the way a side sweep does.
hair.color: Leave it. Near-black is a Dark Winter's own colour and the high contrast against the skin is the asset. If it is ever touched, a cool dark brown — ash or espresso, never caramel or warm brown.
hair.product: Matte clay, not gel — a pea-sized amount worked through towel-dried hair with fingers, lifting from underneath at the crown. Under a minute; the taper does the work, the product just holds it rather than restyling it daily.
hair.why: Vertical lift lengthens the face and gives the jaw its line back; a taper keeps that lift without a two-block's upkeep cost, which is more than wanted for a routine redone every morning and a cut redone every few weeks. The colour advice here used to say the opposite — soften the black to a warm brown — and the undertone test overturned it. That recommendation was warm-season reasoning applied to cool skin, and it was the one thing in this file genuinely riding on the answer. The cut is unaffected: it comes from face shape and upkeep, not colouring.

palette.confidence: Settled for metal, not for every fabric. Depth and contrast were never in doubt. The gold-versus-silver test (2026-09-05) is the strongest-supported claim in here for metal specifically — reflective gold at the jaw is a definite no, silver reads clean — and that rule is not in question. What was overreached was extending it to every warm-toned fabric: on 2026-09-06 he reported his own camel coat and khaki both suit him, which a metal test cannot actually rule out. A polished gold ring returns raw, saturated warmth straight onto the skin; a matte wool coat is muted and sits further from the face, and depth/muting can outweigh hue in a way a mirror shows and a metal swatch cannot. So: metal is a closed question, cool only. Fabric neutrals are open beyond the deep core — camel and khaki are back in, on his word, and nothing else warm has been tested. Charcoal is a different kind of open question: it's cool, so the undertone test never argued against it, but he owns exactly one charcoal item and isn't sure it works. Navy carries the 'default cool neutral' job instead, until charcoal gets the same kind of real-world confirmation camel and khaki got — see `unconfirmed`.
palette.established: Near-black hair, dark brown eyes, light-to-medium skin, high hair-to-skin contrast. Deep colours hold across every lighting seen so far — black and navy both sit at the face without draining it.
palette.resolved: Cool for metal: silver at the face reads clean, gold pulls yellow into the skin. Dark Winter depth and contrast stand regardless. Fabric is less absolute than metal — see `warmNeutrals` below for the two colours his own mirror has already settled.
palette.rule: Deep tones throughout, and let the contrast stand. Black is a real neutral here, mid tones are not. Navy and true white are the cool default; camel and khaki are allowed too, on his own report — see `warmNeutrals`. Charcoal stays unconfirmed — see `unconfirmed`.
palette.metal: Silver, steel, white gold, gunmetal — not gold. Watch, belt buckle, glasses frames, any ring. Metal only; doesn't extend to camel or khaki fabric.

accent.note: Where colour is allowed in an otherwise dark wardrobe.

warmNeutrals.note: Confirmed on his own word, 2026-09-06 — not a metal-test result.

unconfirmed.note: Cool-toned, so never ruled out on undertone grounds — just never actually worn enough to say it works. Navy took over as the default cool neutral instead of waiting on it.

colors.why: One charcoal suit, and he's not sure it suits him — 2026-09-08. The same unconfirmed status khaki had before 2026-09-06; it may well come back in, on the same terms — his own report, not a swatch test.

imageStyle.adaptedFrom: Originally the Teaching Hub house style verbatim — 'black and white graphic novel illustration, bold clean ink lines, no grey gradients'. Moved further on 2026-09-06: 'graphic novel' as a phrase kept pulling image generators toward glossy webtoon/manhwa romance-comic rendering regardless of the negative instructions stacked against it — confirmed when a generated School day image came back with soft gradient shading and an invented chest pocket despite both being explicitly excluded. The prompt now anchors on 'fashion technical flat / croquis', a real, well-represented illustration genre that is inherently flat and unornamented, rather than fighting a genre (graphic novel) whose dominant training association is the opposite of what this page needs.
imageStyle.deviation: Colour is still the one deliberate addition on top of the reference genre: a fashion croquis is normally colourless, but on a wardrobe page the colour IS the content — an emerald knit under a navy overshirt is the whole point — so garments are filled flat in the palette hexes instead.

correction.problem: The first two renders (school-day, parent-evening) came back reading as modern preppy / dark academia — glossy K-webtoon shading and doe-eyed rendering rather than the graphic-novel ink asked for, a flapped topstitched chest pocket, a button-down collar, and trousers with a visible break at the shoe. None of that was written into the prompt; the generator defaulted to the dominant house style for 'handsome young Asian man' illustrations, which is exactly that look. The palette and garments were correct — the rendering and a few unstated details were not.
correction.fix: prefix and figure below now say explicitly what they used to leave to chance: matte flat ink, no glossy or anime/webtoon shading, no doe-eyed romance-comic rendering, matte textured hair rather than a glossy side part, no decorative top-stitching or flapped pockets, no crease-break at the shoe. The parent-evening shirt keeps its collar — a plain spread collar is exactly right under an open coat — but loses the button-down oxford collar (the version with buttons at the points), which is the specific detail that read Ivy. This is not a new direction — it is the one already written in `direction` and `hair`, enforced in the prompt instead of assumed.
correction.existingImages: school-day.png and parent-evening.png predate this fix and were not regenerated — that is a real cost, not a rounding error, and worth redoing only if the drift bothers him enough to spend the effort again.

imageStyle.prefix: A fashion technical flat sketch — a designer's croquis, the plain reference drawing used in clothing design to show a garment on a figure with no artistic rendering. Flat matte black ink outlines of even weight on plain solid colour fills, exactly like a Uniqlo or Muji style guide diagram, not a character illustration, not a graphic novel panel, not anime or webtoon art. No cross-hatching, no soft cel-shading, no grey gradients, no glossy highlights anywhere, on hair or skin or fabric. No fabric texture, no wrinkles, no rendering of any kind — every garment is a single flat shape. Every garment is plain and unornamented: no pockets, no flaps, no stitching detail, no seams drawn in, no visible branding. Plain white background, no scenery, no props, no shadow on the ground. No text, no labels, no captions, no logos.
imageStyle.figure: The same man in all five images so they read as one series: early-30s East Asian man, slim athletic build, light-to-medium skin tone — not pale, not fair-skinned. Mature and quiet rather than boyish or doe-eyed, calm neutral expression with no smile. Near-black hair with length and volume on top and tapered sides, matte and textured with natural separation — not glossy, not a slicked or glassy side part. Standing straight and facing the viewer, arms relaxed at his sides, full body visible from head to shoes, in realistic body proportions — not the elongated 9-head fashion-croquis convention of extra-long legs; keep the leg length true to life relative to the torso. Trousers fall in one continuous straight line with no crease and no break at the shoe.
imageStyle.suffix: Portrait orientation, roughly 3:4. The whole figure must fit inside the frame with clear margin above the head and below the shoes.
imageStyle.howToUse: Concatenate prefix + figure + the look's own `imagePrompt` + suffix, generate, and drop the file into hub/style/img/ named after the occasion slug — school-day.png, parent-evening.png, weekend.png, evening-out.png, colour-carefully.png. The build picks it up on the next run and replaces the drawn placeholder; .png, .jpg and .webp are all accepted.
imageStyle.background: A transparent background is better than white if the generator can do it, because the page has a dark theme as well as a light one. If it cannot, white is fine — the build puts the image on its own white plate so it looks deliberate in both themes rather than like a bug.

rules.why: Hip 105 cm over waist 80 cm is a 25 cm drop. A slim cut pulls at the seat and advertises exactly the ratio the training is working on; straight falls clear of the hip and lengthens the leg.
The taper is being built in the gym. Outerwear with a real shoulder seam — overshirt, coat, unstructured blazer — anticipates it instead of waiting for it.
One depth of colour head to foot reads as height. Splitting light-over-dark cuts the body in half at the waist, which is the one place not to draw a line.
A long unbroken vertical is the most reliable lengthening device there is. Double-breasted adds width across the chest and works against it.

rules.rule: No visible athletic branding outside the gym — heritage fashion branding is a different thing
rules.why: Sport logos say 'on the way to train'; the clothes should not be doing that when the destination is a classroom. That was never a rule against branding as such — a Ralph Lauren pony is a heritage signifier central to this exact register, not a sport logo, and modern preppy is built partly around wearing it visibly. Adidas terrace sneakers (Samba, Barreda) sit in between and were already allowed on their own terms: the branding is subtle by design, not because branding got a pass.

rules.rule: Relaxed, never skinny — and never baggy
rules.why: Easy through the leg, clean at the line. Tight reads dated and fights the hip; oversized reads borrowed and loses the shoulder the whole silhouette is built on.

buyNext.colors: Navy or forest — navy replaces charcoal, unconfirmed for him; forest replaces the deep olive this used to say
buyNext.why: Replaces the printed sweatshirt outright. The slight shoulder structure does work a sweatshirt physically cannot, and it goes over anything already in the wardrobe.
Confirmed 2026-09-06 as the actual work base — a crew neck doesn't belong at school for him, whatever it does off-duty. Charles Tyrwhitt is already on the brand list at the right collar size.

seasonalWardrobe.note: Rewritten 2026-09-05 into the target register, then corrected the same day when the undertone test came back cool — cream, stone, camel, chocolate, tortoise and dark brown all removed. The four-season structure, the straight-leg correction and the tonal-column rule are unchanged throughout.
seasonalWardrobe.styleNote: Natural fabrics — wool, cotton, leather. The rule that carries every season: one depth of colour throughout, a defined shoulder on whatever is outermost. Neutrals default cool — navy and true white — with camel and khaki confirmed as the two exceptions. Charcoal stays unconfirmed.

chinoPlan.goal: End goal: capsule wardrobe largely in Ralph Lauren. This used to be framed as a collector's habit tolerated despite the styling, back when the register was quiet minimalism. Under modern preppy it is the opposite — Ralph Lauren is close to the definitive brand for this register, so wanting it and the styling actually agreeing is the correction, not a coincidence.
chinoPlan.midGoal: Realised differently than planned: Dockers got skipped entirely, and Suitsupply is already the everyday tier, in khaki and navy. Ralph Lauren stays the premium end goal.
chinoPlan.fit: Straight leg, mid-to-high rise. Ask for the straight or relaxed cut by fit, not by model name.

revision.change: The phased 'cheap first, upgrade later' plan didn't happen — he skipped Dockers and bought Suitsupply straight away, in khaki and navy. Charcoal is dropped from every remaining phase: he owns exactly one charcoal item, isn't sure it suits him, and navy is what he actually reaches for. The 2026-09-05 fit and colour corrections (straight leg, khaki back in) still stand.
revision.why: Two separate things converged. The Suitsupply jump is just what happened — the plan is worth updating to match rather than pretending the Dockers step is still 'next'. The charcoal drop is the same rule this file already used for camel and khaki, applied in the other direction: colour that isn't backed by real worn experience doesn't get to sit in the plan as a default, whichever way the theory points.
